subject: Baseline hosted pricing and how input/output/system/tool tokens are counted
messages:
From: Sara Park <sara@acmerobotics.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>, Jordan Blake <jordan@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-01-18T09:02:00-08:00
Subject: Baseline hosted pricing & token counting for streaming tools

Hi Lauren / Jordan,

We're finalizing our evaluation of Redwood for several product surfaces and need a clear baseline on hosted pricing mechanics before we lock a commitment. A few specific things our finance and infra teams want documented:

1) For requests that involve a system prompt + user prompt + tool invocation that returns content (e.g., a reranker or external tool): how are tokens allocated between input vs output? Are system prompts counted as input or separately?

2) Tool outputs: if an external tool returns a 2,400-token JSON blob that we then feed back into the model, how is that charged? Is it billed only once as output tokens, or do we get double-charged when the model ingests it?

3) Streaming and rounding: we stream partial responses to the client. Does Redwood round per-stream-chunk or per-request? If we send ~43.2 tokens worth of audio->text and receive ~44.7 tokens of model output, how will rounding/prorating be reflected on the invoice?

4) Do you apply any minimum-per-request or per-message rounding (e.g., always round up to 1 token or to 8 tokens)?

5) Example invoice: can you provide a sample invoice showing how a single session with 10 requests (mix of tool calls, streaming, and plain chat) would appear with token breakdown and effective unit rates? We're trying to model 50M tokens/month committed pricing and want to see the math.

Attached is a spreadsheet with 4 representative request traces (short/long/system+tool cases). Please point us to the canonical rate card and give a short worked example for each trace.

Thanks — looking forward to a quick turn so procurement can move.

Sara Park
Sr. Platform Engineer, Acme Robotics
--Attachment: Acme_token_examples.xlsx (XLSX, 24KB)
From: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>
To: Sara Park <sara@acmerobotics.com>
Cc: Jordan Blake <jordan@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-01-18T10:15:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Baseline hosted pricing & token counting for streaming tools

Hi Sara — thanks for the clear examples and spreadsheet. Short answers up front, followed by next steps:

- System prompts: counted as input tokens (they are part of the request payload).
- Tool outputs: billed as output tokens at the moment the model returns them; if you then send the tool output back into the model as a subsequent request, those tokens are counted again as input for that new request (so both appearances are chargeable).
- Streaming/rounding: we perform per-request rounding (we round the total input and total output token counts for each request to the nearest integer). We do not round per streaming chunk.
- Minimums: there is no per-request minimum beyond 1 token if a request truly has zero tokens, but typical model responses will rarely hit that.

I've attached our latest hosted rate card (redwood_ratecard_v2.pdf) and a short sample invoice CSV to illustrate. I'll loop in Jordan (sales engineer) for worked numeric examples and then escalate to pricing for a committed-volume illustration and discount cadence.

Would you be able to confirm timezone for your finance review next Tuesday? If you can also flag which of the 4 traces in the spreadsheet are highest priority, Jordan will prioritize those.

Best,
Lauren Bishop
Head of Sales, Redwood Inference
--Attachment: redwood_ratecard_v2.pdf (PDF, 78KB)
From: Jordan Blake <jordan@redwood.com>
To: Sara Park <sara@acmerobotics.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-01-18T11:05:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Baseline hosted pricing & token counting for streaming tools

Sara — looping through your 4 traces quickly and giving worked examples here (short, concrete):

Trace A — short chat + system prompt (no tool):
- System prompt: 64 tokens (counted as input)
- User prompt: 28 tokens (input)
- Model output: 132.3 tokens (output)
Billing: round input total (64+28)=92 tokens; round output=132 tokens. Charged 92 input tokens + 132 output tokens.

Trace B — tool call where tool returns 2,400 tokens and that's fed back in new request:
- Request 1: user prompt 40 tokens, model calls tool -> tool returns 2,400 tokens. Billing: input=40, output=2400.
- Request 2: you POST the tool result into a follow-up prompt which includes the 2,400 tokens as input: input=2400 + follow-up prompt tokens. Billing: you will see the 2,400 tokens again as input on that second request.

Trace C — streaming partial responses (client receives partials):
- Model emits a stream that contains fragments totaling 44.7 tokens. We aggregate the stream server-side and then round the final output token count for that request. So you'll be charged 45 tokens for output for that request (we do not round per fragment).

Trace D — system prompt + tool + rerank (mixed): worked math is attached as a CSV sample (see example-invoice.csv) with per-request lines showing input_token_count, output_token_count, round(input), round(output), unit_rate, line_total.

Rounding policy notes: we do integer rounding of token counts per request (round to nearest integer). For edge ties (x.5) we round up. We do not apply bucketed minimums beyond the effective per-token pricing.

I'll prepare a 50M tokens/month committed example with tiered discount applied and send by EOD. If you want, we can show the difference between: (A) treating tool outputs as billable only when returned to the customer vs (B) billable always when emitted by the model — currently our policy is (B) (emitted outputs are billed when generated; re-ingested tokens are billed again).

—Jordan
Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Sara Park <sara@acmerobotics.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>, Jordan Blake <jordan@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-01-18T14:32:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Baseline hosted pricing & token counting for streaming tools

Thanks — that's helpful and clearer than our procurement expected. A couple follow-ups before we lock a commitment:

- For Trace B (tool output re-ingested): we'd like to propose an alternative commercial treatment where tool outputs used only for post-processing (not shown to end users) are discounted or only counted once. Would Redwood consider a blended-rate for tool-only internal data?

- For the 50M token committed tier: can you provide an illustrative effective per-1k-token rate after the commitment discount and any applied marketplace fees? Our procurement needs an easy line item they can push to finance (we'll need an example PO + sample invoice).

- Also, any SLA considerations if we push >2k RPS with streaming? Is there a different pricing band for high qps streaming workloads?

If you can route this to pricing with the worked examples and a short statement on whether the tool-output-as-input double-counting can be moderated commercially, we can move to an LOI this week.

Tom Li (CC'd) will be the procurement contact.

Sara

Subject: Re: Baseline hosted pricing & token counting for streaming tools

Sara / Tom — thanks for the clear direction. I'm looping in Markus (pricing) and Jonas (sales ops) to propose a commercial path. High level:

1) Commercial proposal (50M tokens/mo):
- List price unit: $0.0022 per 1k input token / $0.0030 per 1k output token (see attached rate card).
- Commitment discount: 28% on listed unit rates at 50M monthly committed volume for a 12-month term.
- Blended effective: roughly $0.001584 per 1k input / $0.00216 per 1k output (illustrative; exact depends on your usage split).

2) Tool-output re-ingestion ask: Markus — can you confirm whether risk/abuse + cost assumptions allow a concession where tool-only internal outputs are billed at 50% when they are never surfaced to end-users? If acceptable we'll surface this as a special term in the SOW.

3) High QPS streaming: our Dedicated offering has an SLA and a predictable pricing band for high RPS/streaming workloads. For hosted, we have burst limits; above sustained 2k RPS we recommend Dedicated or a hybrid routing policy (we can include a burst buffer in the SOW).

4) Next steps: Jonas will prepare a sample PO + example invoice (CSV) that maps the 10-request session from Jordan to the commitment pricing so your finance team can see the line items. Expect the draft LOI/SOW template by EOD today.

I'll follow up with the formal SOW and the special-term language if Markus confirms the tool-output concession.

Best,
Lauren Bishop
Head of Sales, Redwood Inference
